opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think chess is actually a really revealing test case, precisely because it's a domain where the rules are crisp and fully specified. You can write them down on a single page. And what you see with GPT-4 is that it can often play something that *looks* like reasonable chess for a while, especially in the opening, because there's an enormous amount of chess text on the internet. Opening theory, annotated games, commentary. So it's very good at reproducing familiar sequences.

But then you get into the middlegame, into positions that aren't well represented in the training data, and it starts doing things like making illegal moves. Moving a bishop like a knight, castling through check, resurrecting pieces that were already captured. And to me that's the tell. A system that actually had an internal model of the board, that had genuinely abstracted the rules, wouldn't do that. Ever. A seven-year-old who's learned chess for a week doesn't make illegal moves at that rate.

So what it tells you is that the system is approximating the statistics of chess text rather than representing the game itself. It's mimicry rather than understanding. And people will say, "Well, it got to some Elo rating," but the Elo isn't the point. The point is the kind of errors. Illegal moves show that it hasn't induced the rules from millions of examples, which is something humans do from a handful.

And this generalizes. If you can't reliably learn the rules of chess from vast amounts of data, why would we trust these systems to reliably follow the rules of law, or medicine, or arithmetic in novel situations? That's really the deeper issue. It's not about chess per se; it's about whether these systems build stable world models, and chess is a nice, clean demonstration that they mostly don't.

Now, of course, we've had superhuman chess engines for decades. Stockfish, AlphaZero. But those have explicit representations of the board and the rules built in, plus search. That's sort of my whole argument in miniature: you need structure, you need symbolic representation, combined with learning. Pure next-token prediction alone doesn't get you there.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually a really revealing case. People got very excited when GPT-4 came out and it could play what looked like reasonable chess for a while, and then you'd see it make an illegal move. It would move a bishop through a pawn, or castle when the king had already moved, or it would just conjure a piece onto a square where it had no business being. And the thing is, if you actually understood chess, you would never do that. A seven-year-old who's been taught the rules doesn't move a knight like a rook. They might play badly, but they don't violate the rules of the game, because they have an internal model of what the game is.

So what GPT-4 is doing is what it always does. It's predicting plausible continuations of text. It's seen millions of PGN transcripts, it knows what sequences of moves tend to follow other sequences, and in the openings, where the data is dense, that works pretty well. Get into a novel middlegame position, something it hasn't effectively memorized, and it falls apart, because it never actually built a representation of the board. There's no board in there. There's no notion of "this square is occupied." It's approximating chess from the outside rather than understanding it from the inside.

And I think this is emblematic of the broader problem. It's not that these systems are useless, and it's not that they'll never get better at chess with more data or with tool use, where you bolt on an actual engine. But the pattern, where the system looks competent on the distribution it's seen and then fails in ways no genuinely competent agent would fail, that's the signature of a system without a world model. We saw it with chess, we see it with arithmetic, we see it with hallucinated citations. It's the same thing over and over. And my worry is that people keep mistaking fluency for comprehension. Chess is just a nice, crisp place where you can see the difference clearly, because the rules are explicit and the errors are unambiguous.

astra-6.text: I’d distinguish producing plausible chess moves from reliably playing chess. A language model might reproduce an opening because it has seen many examples, but that doesn’t establish that it consistently tracks the board, respects the rules, or plans ahead. You’d want to test those things over complete games, including unfamiliar positions. If it makes an illegal move, that’s revealing: it suggests a gap between generating something that looks like chess and maintaining the state of the game. And if you connect it to a chess engine, you need to distinguish the engine’s competence from the language model’s.

sol-6.1.text: I’d distinguish between talking about chess and actually playing it. GPT-4 can produce a plausible explanation of an opening because it has seen lots of chess notation and commentary. But maintaining the board position over a game, tracking which moves are legal, and planning reliably are different matters. It can make illegal moves or lose track of where the pieces are. That suggests it hasn’t acquired a sufficiently robust model of the game. Hook it up to a chess engine and you can get excellent play, but then you have to ask which component is doing the work.
